summary.text: A mineral's streak is the color of the powder it leaves when dragged across an unweathered surface, usually an unglazed porcelain streak plate.
It is an important identification tool because the powder's color is generally more consistent than a mineral's outward color, which can vary a lot.
Dragging breaks the sample into randomly oriented microscopic crystals, so small impurities do not greatly affect how the powder absorbs light.

facts.label: Hematite's streak
facts.value: Red, though the mineral looks black

facts.label: Fluorite's streak
facts.value: Always white, whatever its crystal color

items.prompt: Hematite looks black. What color powder does it leave on a streak plate?

options.label: Black
Gray
White
Red

items.explain: Black-looking hematite leaves a red streak, which is where its blood-related Greek name comes from.

items.prompt: You find purple and green crystals that turn out to be the same mineral. What most likely explains their different outward colors?

options.label: Traces of impurities in the crystals
One crystal is much older than the other
They formed at different hardnesses
One has been crushed into powder

items.explain: Small amounts of an impurity that strongly absorbs certain wavelengths can radically change a mineral's apparent color.

items.prompt: A shiny dark specimen could be either hematite or galena, which can look alike. Which quick test tells them apart?

options.label: Hold it near a fridge magnet
Rub it on porcelain and check the powder
Look at it under bright sunlight
Weigh it in your hand

items.explain: Hematite leaves a red streak while galena leaves a gray one, so the powder color settles it.

items.prompt: Your mineral is harder than the porcelain plate and leaves no powder trail. How can you still learn its powder color?

options.label: Assume the powder matches its outer color
Press harder until a trail appears
File or crush a bit, then rub that on the plate
Wet the plate so the mineral sticks

items.explain: A streak needs a mineral softer than the plate; for harder ones, filing or crushing a sample gives powder to rub on the plate.

items.prompt: Why is a streak test usually of little help with silicate minerals?

options.label: They dissolve when rubbed on porcelain
Most streak white or are too hard to powder
Their powder changes color in the air
They are always too soft to leave a trail

items.explain: Most silicates have a white streak or resist being powdered, so the test rarely tells them apart.

items.prompt: You have no streak plate with you. Which household item could stand in for one?

options.label: A sheet of window glass
A glossy glazed plate's top surface
A piece of white paper
The unglazed underside of a porcelain bowl

items.explain: The unglazed underside of a porcelain bowl or vase, or the back of a glazed tile, works like a streak plate.
